projects.name: Ground work
projects.summary: Get PR #4 onto main, settle the open calls, and protect the data layer from the sync script.

projects.name: Supabase foundation
projects.summary: Project, migrations, row-level security enforcing owner + two-factor, a private image bucket, generated types.

projects.name: Sign-in and two-factor
projects.summary: Username sign-in through an Edge Function, a real session behind the synchronous getSession(), and TOTP.

projects.name: iOS foundation
projects.summary: The native app exists and can be run on your phone: framework, tokens, navigation, and the motion primitives everything else is built on. No backend dependency, so it runs alongside p1.

projects.name: Library data
projects.summary: Collections, references, notes, tags, pins and uploads move from browser storage to Postgres and Storage.

projects.name: Boards
projects.summary: Publish, rotate and unpublish in Postgres; a signed-out Edge Function serves boards with short-lived image URLs.

projects.name: Invites
projects.summary: Invite requests stored server-side, deduplicated by email, with a notification to you.

projects.name: iOS library
projects.summary: The screens that matter on a phone: collections, the reference grid, the viewer, pins, notes. Built against the contract on mocks, then wired to real data once p3 lands.

projects.name: iOS capture
projects.summary: The reason the app exists: camera, photo library, and Share → Kept from Safari, Photos or Instagram, with an upload queue that survives losing signal.

projects.name: Web v0 ship
projects.summary: Seed moode-matcha into Storage, set env and secrets, re-verify pixel parity and RLS, deploy the web app.

projects.name: iOS ship
projects.summary: Universal Links, the App Store requirements that are not optional (account deletion, privacy manifest, minimum functionality), then TestFlight and review.

projects.name: Later
projects.summary: Worth doing, not needed for v0: box annotations, renaming, server search, share previews, and the bigger platform bets (iPad, widgets, Android, a SwiftUI rewrite if the feel ceiling is ever hit).

options.detail: The browser sends username + password to a function that looks up the email with the service role and signs in server-side. Emails never leave the server, and an unknown username gives the same error as a wrong password.
options.label: Edge Function `sign-in`

options.detail: Each account's email is `username@users.kept.design`. No server code, but no real inbox for recovery or notices.
options.label: Synthetic emails

options.detail: An anon-callable `email_for_username()`. Simplest, but it lets anyone enumerate usernames and read their emails. Not recommended.
options.label: Public lookup function

decisions.question: Kept signs in by username, but Supabase Auth signs in by email. Something has to turn a username into an email without letting anyone look up whose account is whose.
decisions.title: How usernames sign in

options.detail: The function checks the token and returns URLs that expire (about an hour). Unpublish and New link take effect immediately for new visits. One bucket, nothing public.
options.label: Signed URLs from the `board` function

options.detail: Publishing copies files into a public bucket. Links never expire and CDN caching is simpler, but every publish, rotate and unpublish has to copy or delete files.
options.label: Public copies of published images

decisions.question: Library images stay in a private bucket. Boards are opened by people who aren't signed in, so their images need a different path.
decisions.title: How board images are served

options.detail: Billed through Vercel; env vars sync to Production, Preview and Development automatically. Vite only exposes `VITE_`-prefixed vars, so `vite.config` adds the integration's `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_` prefix to `envPrefix`.
options.label: Vercel Marketplace integration

options.detail: Billed by Supabase; env vars are copied into Vercel by hand. Nothing else changes.
options.label: supabase.com directly

decisions.question: Supabase can be created directly on supabase.com or through the Vercel Marketplace integration.
decisions.title: Where Supabase is provisioned

options.detail: `repository.ts` picks the Supabase implementation when configured, else the synced mock. The lab account `wade / 1234` keeps working locally. This matches the v0 spec.
options.label: Fall back to the mocks

options.detail: Simpler code paths, but every preview and fresh clone needs real credentials.
options.label: Require Supabase everywhere

decisions.question: When Supabase env vars are missing (a fresh clone, a preview without secrets), the app can either fall back to kept-ui's mocks or refuse to start.
decisions.title: Keep the mocks as a fallback

options.detail: Delete `public/collections/` from main once KEPT-28 has moved them into Storage. They stay in git history, but the app stops depending on them.
options.label: Remove them after the seed

options.detail: Useful for the mock fallback on previews. Costs repo size and keeps the images public.
options.label: Keep them in the repo

decisions.question: PR #3 already committed the 320 moode-matcha files to main (the repo is public). Once they're in Storage, the copies in `public/collections/` aren't needed.
decisions.title: Collection images in git

options.detail: Real native views. Reanimated runs animations on the UI thread, so gestures track 1:1 and stay interruptible. Keeps React and TypeScript, so the mental model and the data contract carry over. Base UI does not, so the 16 screens are rebuilt. This is what apps like Phantom use.
options.label: React Native

options.detail: The highest ceiling and the most Apple-native feel, at the cost of a new language and paradigm, and the furthest distance from everything already built.
options.label: Native SwiftUI

options.detail: The original `/ios` plan: the Vite build inside a WKWebView. By far the cheapest, and keeps one codebase. Rejected: a web view cannot hold 120fps on a 300-image grid or give interruptible gesture physics, and Kept is exactly that kind of app.
options.label: Capacitor wrapper

decisions.question: The UI rebuild happens once. Capacitor was the original plan, chosen to avoid rebuilding the UI; the goal has since changed to an app that feels genuinely native in the hand, which a web view cannot deliver for an image-heavy, gesture-heavy app.
decisions.title: How the iOS app is built

options.detail: Closes the question. Matches the domain, the repo and everything already written.
options.label: Stay Kept — `design.kept.app`

options.detail: If the name is going to change, this is the cheapest moment in the project's life to do it. Blocks KEPT-40 until it lands.
options.label: Rename before the Xcode project

options.detail: Build on a scratch identifier and replace it before the first external build. Buys time; costs a pass over Universal Links, App Groups and the App Store Connect record.
options.label: Throwaway id now, decide before TestFlight

decisions.question: A bundle identifier is permanent once an app is public: a new one is a new app, with new reviews and no upgrade path for anyone who installed the old one. The display name can change; the identifier cannot. Today this costs nothing to settle.
decisions.title: The app name and bundle identifier

options.detail: Config plugins generate the native project, so custom native code (share extension, App Groups, associated domains) still works. EAS handles signing and TestFlight uploads. Much less Xcode time.
options.label: Expo with a development build

options.detail: Total control of the Xcode project, and no dependency on Expo's release cadence. More setup, more signing work, and every native change is done by hand.
options.label: Bare React Native

decisions.question: React Native can be set up bare or through Expo. The share extension and App Groups both need custom native code, which used to be the reason to avoid Expo and no longer is.
decisions.title: Expo or bare React Native

options.detail: Colors, type scale, spacing and radii move to `tokens.json`, which generates the CSS custom properties for web and a typed object for native. kept-ui stays the source of truth for web layout and design intent; tokens become the source for both.
options.label: Tokens become the shared layer

options.detail: No new tooling. Every token change has to be mirrored into the native app manually, and they will drift.
options.label: kept-ui stays the source, native copies by hand

options.detail: Fastest in the short term, and guarantees the two apps stop looking like the same product.
options.label: Let iOS have its own design system

decisions.question: `tokens.css` is web-only, and Base UI cannot run on iOS. The rule that kept-ui is the single source of truth for the UI was written when there was one renderer, and the rebuild breaks it.
decisions.title: Where the design system lives once there are two renderers

options.detail: Refresh tokens live in the iOS keychain, protected by the device passcode and wiped on uninstall. Supabase's auth client takes a custom storage adapter, so this is a small amount of code.
options.label: Keychain via `expo-secure-store`

options.detail: The common default in React Native examples. It is an unencrypted file in the app container — acceptable for preferences, not for a refresh token that grants access to the whole library.
options.label: `AsyncStorage`

decisions.question: The web app keeps its session in `sessionStorage` so a refresh mid-2FA stays on the MFA step. A phone app is expected to stay signed in for months, which makes the storage choice a security decision rather than a convenience one.
decisions.title: Where the session lives on the device

acceptance: Every field the UI reads maps to a column (see the seam table)

issues.code:
profiles      id uuid pk → auth.users · username citext unique (2–32 [a-z0-9._-])
collections   id uuid pk · owner_id · slug text · name text (≤80) · description text
              created_at · updated_at · unique (owner_id, slug)
refs          id uuid pk · public_id text unique · owner_id · collection_id → collections
              title · notes · capture_url (null = uploaded) · added_at · updated_at
              search tsvector generated
assets        id uuid pk · ref_id → refs (cascade) · owner_id · path_full · path_thumb
              file_name · file_type · width · height · bytes
tags          id uuid pk · owner_id · name citext · unique (owner_id, name)
ref_tags      ref_id → refs · tag_id → tags · pk (ref_id, tag_id)
annotations   id uuid pk · ref_id → refs (cascade) · owner_id · kind ('pin'|'box')
              x · y · w · h (null for pins) · caption · position int
collection_shares  collection_id pk → collections (cascade) · token text unique
                   published_at · rotated_at
invite_requests    id uuid pk · name · email citext unique · note (≤500)
                   requested_at · status ('waiting'|'invited'|'declined')
steps: Write `0001_schema.sql` with the tables below; UUID primary keys, `owner_id` on every row for RLS.
Collections keep a `slug` because the UI uses it as the collection id in URLs (`/library/moode-matcha`). References keep a short `public_id` for `/library/:c/:r`.
`references` is a reserved word in SQL, so the table is `refs`.
Add `updated_at` triggers, and a generated `search` tsvector on refs for later server search (KEPT-34).
issues.summary: Turns the shapes in `repository.ts` into tables. A Reference is the unit of meaning; its Asset carries the file facts; v0 has one asset and one collection per reference.
issues.title: Schema migration

acceptance: pgTAP (or SQL) tests: user B can't select, update or delete user A's rows in any table
An aal1 session reads zero rows
anon reads zero rows from every table
steps: Enable RLS on every table. No policies on `invite_requests` or `collection_shares` for anon.
One permissive policy per table for select/insert/update/delete: `owner_id = auth.uid()`.
One restrictive policy per table: `(auth.jwt() ->> 'aal') = 'aal2'`.
`profiles`: a user reads and updates only their own row; usernames are set by you, not the user.
Signed-out access goes only through SECURITY DEFINER functions with narrow return shapes (board, invite).
issues.summary: The browser talks straight to Postgres, so RLS is the whole security model. Checking `aal2` in the policies means a stolen password without the second factor reads nothing.
issues.title: Row-level security: owner and two-factor on every row

steps: `startTotpEnrollment()` → `auth.mfa.enroll({ factorType: 'totp' })`, returning the QR SVG and secret.
`verifyTotp(code)` → `auth.mfa.challenge()` then `auth.mfa.verify()`; on success refresh the session cache to aal2.
The gate already sends aal1 sessions to `/login/mfa`; the screen shows Set up when no factor is verified, else Verify.
Recovery: Supabase has no backup codes. Enroll a second TOTP factor (another device or a password manager) and document the dashboard reset as the last resort.
issues.summary: Makes the aal2 requirement real. Supabase's MFA API does enroll → challenge → verify and upgrades the session to aal2.

Create the collection `moode-matcha` for `wade`, upload all 160 full and thumb files, insert refs and assets with the file facts from the JSON.
Publish it with the existing token `mm7q2x9kfa` so the board link you've already shared keeps working.
Idempotent: re-running skips what exists.
issues.summary: Your real collection has to move from `public/collections/` and `data/moode-matcha.json` into your account.

acceptance: `grep` of `dist/` finds no service-role key
Previews without secrets fall back to the mocks (D-4)
steps: Vercel (Production + Preview): `VITE_SUPABASE_URL`, `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, `VITE_PUBLIC_ORIGIN`.
Edge Function secrets: service-role key, Resend key.
Local: `.env.local` for the app and the seed script; `.env.example` committed without values.
Check the production bundle for anything that looks like a service key before the first deploy.
issues.summary: Only the publishable key may reach the browser.

acceptance: All three pass on the production project before the domain switch
steps: Re-run the pixel sweep against kept-ui with the same collection seeded: every route and state identical (share URLs excepted).
End to end: sign in → TOTP → create collection → upload → pin → tag → notes → publish → open board signed out → New link → Unpublish → invite request.
RLS tests from KEPT-9 pass against the deployed project.
Log a health run (`health/log.csv`) for the release.
issues.summary: Real data mustn't change how anything looks, and the security model needs proof, not assumption.
issues.title: Verify the web app: pixel parity, end-to-end and RLS

acceptance: kept.design serves the real app with real data
steps: Merge to main → Vercel production deploy.
Point `kept.design` at the project; check `/`, `/library` (signed in), and a board signed out.
Tick “Ship to kept.design” in Kept's own To do page.

issues.summary: Uploads take the file name as the title. Needs an editable title in kept-ui, then `updateReference` accepts `title`.
issues.title: Rename references

issues.summary: A preview card when a board link is pasted into a chat. A tiny OG endpoint for `/m/:token`, without moving the app to Next.js.
issues.title: Board link previews

issues.summary: Out of scope for v0 by design. Revisit only if egress or storage costs become real.
issues.title: Move images to R2 if Storage costs bite

acceptance: D-6 has a chosen option and a recorded reason
`/ios` describes the current plan and contains no stale claims
AGENTS.md says which source of truth applies to which renderer
issues.notes: Nothing in the backend roadmap (p1–p6) is affected by this decision. Schema, RLS, Storage, Auth and both Edge Functions serve a native client exactly as they serve the browser.
steps: Record the call in D-6 with the reasoning, not just the choice.

Rewrite `src/kept/KeptIos.tsx` so `/ios` describes the real plan. Four things in it are already wrong: it says hash routes work unchanged (kept-design uses real paths), it says `pnpm` (this repo is npm), it points at `kept-ui.vercel.app` as "today", and it hardcodes a LAN IP in a public repo.
Rewrite the AGENTS.md rule that kept-ui is the single source of truth for the UI: true for web, false once a second renderer exists.
Write down the condition that would reopen D-6, so it is a test rather than a mood: KEPT-44 failing its frame budget on device.
issues.summary: The `/ios` page in the app still describes a Capacitor wrapper, chosen when the goal was "don't rebuild the UI". The goal is now an app that feels native in the hand, which points somewhere else (D-6). The old plan has to be retired in writing or it will keep resurfacing.
issues.title: Confirm the native framework and retire the Capacitor plan

acceptance: D-7 has a chosen option
The identifier is recorded once and referenced everywhere else
The name is reserved in App Store Connect
issues.notes: The App Store display name can be changed later. The bundle identifier and the App Group identifier cannot, in practice.
steps: Settle D-7.

Pick the reverse-DNS identifier (`design.kept.app` if the name stands) and write it down in exactly one place that the Xcode project, the App Group, the associated domain and App Store Connect all read from.
Reserve the name in App Store Connect once KEPT-39 is done — reservation is first-come and free.
issues.summary: A bundle identifier is permanent once the app is public. Changing it after release means a new App Store listing, new reviews, and no upgrade path for anyone who already installed it. The name question has been open and low-priority; for iOS it stops being low-priority at KEPT-40.
issues.title: Settle the app name and bundle identifier

acceptance: Membership is active
App Store Connect has the app record with the agreed bundle identifier
issues.notes: Enrolling as an individual publishes your legal name as the seller. If that matters, sort out the entity before enrolling rather than after.
steps: Enroll. Individual or company changes the seller name shown publicly on the App Store; switching afterwards is a support process, not a settings toggle.
Two-factor on the Apple ID is mandatory for App Store Connect.
Create the app record in App Store Connect and reserve the name from KEPT-38.
issues.summary: $99 a year. Required for TestFlight, the App Store, Universal Links, App Groups and push. A free Apple ID can only sideload to your own device, and the install expires after seven days — enough to prove KEPT-44, not enough to live with the app.
issues.title: Join the Apple Developer Program

acceptance: A development build runs on your iPhone over the cable
A test animation measurably runs above 60fps on device
The bundle identifier matches KEPT-38 everywhere it appears
issues.code:
app.config.ts
  ios.bundleIdentifier   design.kept.app          (D-7)
  ios.infoPlist          CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone: true
  ios.supportsTablet     false                    (iPad is a later bet)
  plugins                expo-dev-client, expo-font, expo-image,
                         expo-secure-store, expo-image-picker
steps: `npx create-expo-app` with the TypeScript template; add `expo-dev-client` so custom native code is possible from day one.
Set the bundle identifier from KEPT-38 in `app.config.ts`.
Set `CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone` to `YES` in Info.plist. Without it iOS caps the app at 60fps on ProMotion devices and every animation silently loses half its frames.
EAS build profiles: `development` (dev client on device), `preview` (internal distribution), `production` (TestFlight and App Store).
Decide repo layout: a sibling repo, or a folder in a monorepo alongside the web app. The only thing that genuinely needs sharing is tokens (KEPT-41) and the data contract (KEPT-45).
issues.summary: The project itself: Expo with a development build (D-8), TypeScript strict, the agreed bundle identifier, and the one Info.plist flag without which the app is capped at 60fps on a 120Hz phone.
issues.title: Create the React Native app

acceptance: Changing one value in `tokens.json` changes both apps
The web app is pixel-identical before and after the extraction
Native screens reference tokens, never literals
issues.notes: This is the concrete moment kept-ui stops being the single source of truth for the UI. It stays the source for web layout and design intent; tokens become the shared layer beneath both.
steps: Extract `src/kept/tokens.css` into `tokens.json`: colour (light and dark), spacing scale, radii, type scale, weights, and the motion constants from KEPT-44.
A generator emits CSS custom properties for the web app and a typed TS object for native.
The web app keeps importing the generated CSS, so nothing changes visually and the pixel sweep still passes.
Lint rule or review habit: no raw hex, no magic spacing numbers in native screen code.
issues.summary: `tokens.css` is web-only, so today there is no way for the two apps to agree on a colour. Implements D-9: one source of truth that generates both.
issues.title: Design tokens as shared data

acceptance: Every web route has a native counterpart or a written "not on phone"
The navigation shape is approved before any library screen is built
issues.notes: Kept's job on a phone is capture and browse. The long tail of account screens can be thin or absent without hurting the product.
steps: Decide the root: a tab bar (Library · Search · Add · You) or a single stack with a prominent capture action.
Map each of the 16 web routes to a native screen, a sheet, or explicitly nothing. `/map`, `/ios`, `/todo` and `/referral` are almost certainly nothing.
Decide what a modal sheet is and what is a pushed screen — a rule, applied consistently, not a per-screen judgement call.
Design it before building it. Whether that is kept-ui, Figma or paper matters less than it being approved before KEPT-46 starts.
issues.summary: The web app is a three-pane desktop layout across 16 routes. A phone is not a small desktop: the screens have to be re-planned, not ported. Getting this wrong is expensive because every later screen sits inside it.
issues.title: Native information architecture

acceptance: Light and dark match the web tokens side by side
Nothing is obscured by the notch or the home indicator on a modern iPhone
Text at the largest accessibility size is still usable
steps: Load Geist and Geist Mono with `expo-font`; fall back to the system face while they load rather than flashing.
Light and dark from `useColorScheme`, reading the same tokens as the web (KEPT-41).
Safe areas with `react-native-safe-area-context` — the notch, the home indicator, and the keyboard.
Decide the Dynamic Type position: full support, or a capped scale. Accessibility text sizes will break a dense image grid if ignored entirely.
issues.summary: The chrome that makes a native app feel like it belongs to the same product as the website.
issues.title: Type, fonts, dark mode and safe areas

acceptance: A scroll of 300 images holds 120fps on device
A sheet can be caught mid-animation and reversed without snapping
Nothing animates through React state
issues.notes: If this issue cannot hit its frame budget, D-6 gets reopened here — before sixteen screens are built on top of it, not after.
steps: `react-native-reanimated` and `react-native-gesture-handler`. Every animation runs on the UI thread from a shared value — never driven by React state, which puts it back on the JS thread and back at the mercy of a render.
One shared spring configuration in tokens, so every surface in the app decelerates the same way.
The rule, written down: every animation is interruptible. Anything you can start with a gesture, you can catch mid-flight and reverse.
Velocity carries from the gesture into the animation. A flung sheet keeps the speed of the finger that threw it.
Build a throwaway test screen: 300 images, fast scroll, a pinch, a drag-dismiss. Profile it on a real device, not the simulator.
Load the `apple-design` and `gesture-ui` guidance before setting the spring values, rather than guessing at numbers.
issues.summary: The whole reason for rebuilding instead of wrapping. These primitives get set once, before any screen depends on them, and they are also the test of whether the framework choice was right.
issues.title: Motion and gesture foundations

acceptance: Native screens compile against the same types the web app uses
Every p9 screen runs on mocks with no backend
Swapping mocks for Supabase touches one module
issues.notes: Depends on KEPT-11 only for the generated types. Everything else here can start immediately.
steps: Same function names and return shapes as the web: `listCollections`, `getCollection`, `listReferences`, `updateReference`, `addUploads`, `getSession`, `signInWithPassword`.
Share the generated database types from KEPT-11 rather than redeclaring them; a drift here should fail a typecheck, not surface as a bug.
`supabase-js` in React Native needs `react-native-url-polyfill` and a storage adapter for auth — the keychain one from D-10.
Port the mock repository so every screen in p9 can be built and demoed before p3 lands.
issues.summary: The seam is the most valuable thing in the web repo: screens call `repository.ts` and `session.ts`, and swapping mocks for Supabase touches no screen. The native app gets the same seam, so its screens can be built on mocks while the backend is still being built.
issues.title: The data contract on native

acceptance: Matches the approved KEPT-42 design
Runs entirely on mocks
Cold open to interactive in under a second on device
steps: Collection list or grid with cover images and counts.
Pull to refresh; empty state; skeletons that match the token type scale rather than generic grey bars.
Create a collection from here, as a sheet.
Open transition into a collection uses the shared spring, not a stock push.
issues.summary: The root screen: your collections, and a way into All references. The first screen built on the KEPT-42 navigation and the KEPT-44 primitives, so it is also where both get proven.
issues.title: Collections home

acceptance: 300+ references scroll at 120fps on device with no blank tiles
Memory stays flat over a long scroll; the app is not jetsammed
A cold open with a warm disk cache shows images without a flash
issues.notes: This is the issue that proves or disproves the whole rebuild. Worth profiling on the oldest phone you intend to support, not just yours.
steps: `@shopify/flash-list` for recycling. A plain list keeps every row mounted and will not survive a real library.
`expo-image` for decode and caching — it is backed by SDWebImage on iOS and handles memory and disk caching properly.
Thumbnails in the grid (480px), never the full image. The full 1600px asset is only ever loaded by the viewer.
Prefetch ahead of the scroll direction; cancel prefetches that scroll past.
Set an explicit memory ceiling for the image cache and test against the largest collection, not a demo one.
Fixed aspect tiles or a measured masonry layout — decide before building, since masonry with recycling is materially harder.
issues.summary: The screen Kept lives or dies on, and the one a web view could never do properly: hundreds of images, scrolled fast, at 120fps, without the app being killed for memory. moode-matcha alone is 320 files.
issues.title: The reference grid

acceptance: Pinch tracks the fingers with no perceptible lag
A dismiss can be reversed mid-flight
The image lands exactly on its grid tile when it returns
Holds 120fps throughout on device
issues.notes: Load the `apple-design` and `gesture-ui` guidance before building this one. It is the issue most worth over-investing in.
steps: Shared-element transition from the grid tile into the viewer: the tile becomes the image, it does not cross-fade.
Pinch to zoom with two-finger pan, tracking the fingers exactly, with rubber-banding past the bounds and a spring back.
Drag down to dismiss, with the background dimming in proportion to the drag and the image returning to its tile if released early.
Velocity decides the outcome: a fast flick dismisses even from a short distance.
Every part of it interruptible — you can catch a dismissing image and drag it back.
issues.summary: Opening a reference is the most-repeated gesture in the app. It is also the clearest single signal of whether an app feels native, because everyone has Photos.app as a reference point.
issues.title: Reference viewer: pinch, pan and drag to dismiss

acceptance: Swiping through twenty references never shows a loading state
Dismissing lands on the correct tile after paging
Zoomed panning never accidentally pages
steps: Horizontal paging within the viewer, sharing the zoom state machine from KEPT-48 so a zoomed image pans instead of paging.
Preload the neighbours on both sides; release images more than two away.
Keep the grid's scroll position in sync, so dismissing returns you to the reference you ended on rather than the one you started from.
issues.summary: Once a reference is open, moving to the next one should be a flick, not a trip back to the grid.
issues.title: Swipe between references

acceptance: A pin can be placed accurately at the top and bottom edges of the image
Pin positions match the web app exactly for the same reference
Captions are readable and editable with the keyboard up
steps: Long-press to place, drag to position, with the pin offset above the finger so it is not hidden by it.
A magnifier or offset preview while dragging, since the finger covers the target.
Caption entry as a sheet, with the keyboard handled so the pin stays visible.
Haptic on placement and on hitting a snap threshold, not on every frame of the drag.
Pins live in image coordinates, not screen coordinates, so they survive zoom and rotation.
issues.summary: Pins are what make a reference a reference rather than a photo. Placing one on a phone is a different interaction from placing one with a mouse.
issues.title: Pins on native

acceptance: The caret is never hidden behind the keyboard
Dismissing the sheet mid-edit does not lose the edit
Tags created on the phone appear on the web and the reverse
steps: Notes as a sheet with the keyboard pushing content rather than covering it.
Tag entry with autocomplete from existing tags; creating a tag is the same gesture as picking one.
Save on dismiss, not with an explicit Save button; show that it saved without a modal.
Same field-level errors and copy as the web app.
issues.summary: The editing surfaces. Mostly unremarkable, except that keyboard handling on iOS is where otherwise-good apps fall apart.
issues.title: Notes, tags and titles

acceptance: Search over a 500-reference library stays responsive while typing
Results match the web app for the same query
steps: Filter across titles, notes, tags and pin captions — the same fields the web filters.
Debounced, running off the main thread if the library is large.
Recent searches; an empty state that offers something rather than shrugging.
issues.summary: Matches the web app's v0 position (KEPT-22): filter what is already loaded rather than build server search. Revisit with KEPT-34 when either client outgrows it.
issues.title: Search on device

acceptance: 120fps held across the main flows on device
Reduce Motion produces a calm app, not a broken one
No default-looking transitions remain
issues.notes: This is the issue that the whole rebuild was justified by. If it gets cut for time, the rebuild was not worth doing.
steps: Haptics bound to gesture thresholds and state changes, never to taps for their own sake. A haptic that fires on everything stops meaning anything.
Audit every transition for interruptibility; anything that cannot be caught mid-flight gets rebuilt.
Remove every stock animation that was left at its default while building.
Check the whole app under Reduce Motion: every spring becomes a fade, nothing becomes a jump.
Profile on device, holding 120fps through the grid, the viewer and every sheet.
Hand the app to someone who has not seen it and watch where their thumb hesitates.
issues.summary: A dedicated pass over the whole app for the things that separate "works" from "feels amazing". Deliberately its own issue, because polish that is left as a sub-task of every other issue never happens.
issues.title: The feel pass

acceptance: Airplane mode still shows previously-browsed collections and thumbnails
Expired signed URLs re-sign without the user noticing
The cache respects its ceiling over a week of real use
steps: Disk cache for thumbnails with an explicit size ceiling and an eviction policy.
Cache collection and reference metadata so the grid renders offline even when images are still arriving.
Signed Storage URLs expire — cache the image bytes, never the URL, and re-sign on demand.
An honest offline state: show what is cached, say what is not, never an infinite spinner.
issues.summary: A phone loses signal. A reference library that goes blank on the underground is not a library you trust.
issues.title: Image cache and offline reads

acceptance: A collection made on the phone appears on the web without a reload, and the reverse
The app stays signed in across relaunches and a week of backgrounding
RLS holds from the native client, tested with a second account
steps: Swap the mock adapter for the Supabase implementation behind the KEPT-45 contract — one module, no screen changes.
Sign-in through the same `sign-in` Edge Function as the web, then TOTP to reach AAL2.
Session in the keychain (D-10), with refresh handled on resume so the app is not signed out after a week in the background.
Verify row-level security from the device: a second account must see nothing of yours.
issues.summary: The moment the phone and the web become one product: the same account, the same collections, the same images, from either device. This is what "sign into the website and see what I collected on my phone" actually means.
issues.title: Wire the native library to Supabase

acceptance: A photo goes from camera to a collection in two taps
Limited photo access works without repeated prompting
Uploads from the phone are byte-comparable to the same file uploaded on the web
steps: `expo-image-picker` for camera and library, with multi-select from the library.
Permission strings in Info.plist written in Kept's voice — they are user-facing copy, not boilerplate.
Use the limited photo library selection properly; do not nag for full access.
Reuse the existing on-device resize (1600px full, 480px thumb, metadata stripped) so phone uploads match web uploads exactly.
Strip location metadata. A reference library has no business recording where a photo was taken.
issues.summary: The most obvious thing an app can do that a website cannot: put what is in front of you, or already on your phone, into a collection in two taps.
issues.title: Camera and photo library import

acceptance: Share → Kept works from Safari, Photos and Instagram
A shared URL lands as a reference with its capture URL set
Sharing ten large photos at once does not crash the extension
The destination collection can be chosen without opening the app
issues.notes: The biggest single piece of native work in the plan, and the one that most changes how Kept is used day to day.
steps: A share extension target, added through an Expo config plugin (D-8) so it survives a prebuild.
Accept images, URLs and text. A shared URL becomes a reference with `capture_url` set, matching the web's captured references.
Pick a destination collection inside the extension, without launching the app.
Extensions get a hard memory limit — around 120MB — and are killed without ceremony. Hand large images off rather than processing them in the extension.
The extension UI is small: it must still look like Kept, using the shared tokens.
issues.summary: The single best reason for this app to exist. Share → Kept from Safari, Photos or Instagram is how a visual reference library actually gets filled, and it is also what makes the app more than a website in a wrapper under App Store guideline 4.2.
issues.title: Share extension

acceptance: The app picks up items shared while it was closed
The extension knows the signed-in account
Nothing accumulates indefinitely in the shared container
steps: Create the App Group identifier alongside the bundle identifier (KEPT-38); like the bundle id, it is painful to change later.
Shared container for handed-off files; shared defaults for the queue.
The extension writes to the container and enqueues; the app drains the queue on next launch or resume.
Share the auth session across the group so the extension knows who is signed in without its own sign-in flow.
Clean up handed-off files after a successful upload, and on a schedule for ones that failed.
issues.summary: A share extension is a separate process with its own sandbox. An App Group is the only way it can hand files and state to the app.
issues.title: App Group handoff

acceptance: Twenty photos queued, app backgrounded immediately, all arrive
Killing the app mid-upload loses nothing; it resumes on next launch
Airplane mode queues and drains automatically on reconnect
One corrupt file fails alone, with no orphan rows or objects
steps: A persistent queue that survives app termination — on disk, not in memory.
Per-item state matching the web's upload dialog: Waiting, Adding…, Added, failed. Same copy, same running count.
Background upload via `URLSession` background transfers so uploads continue after the app is suspended.
Retry with backoff; distinguish a failed file from a lost connection and say which.
One failure never takes down the batch — the web app's rule, kept.
Show the queue somewhere honest. An upload silently failing is worse than one visibly retrying.
issues.summary: Phone uploads are not desktop uploads: the network drops, the app gets backgrounded, and iOS suspends processes without warning. An upload that only works in the foreground on good wifi is not an upload.
issues.title: Upload queue and background uploads

acceptance: Sharing a board offers Messages, Mail and the rest
The shared link is the public kept.design URL
steps: The native share sheet for a published board link.
Links use `https://kept.design/m/…` (KEPT-25), never a local or preview origin.
Keep copy-to-clipboard as the secondary action, with the native haptic confirmation.
issues.summary: Publishing a board on the phone should hand you the system share sheet, not a copy-to-clipboard toast borrowed from the web.
issues.title: Native share sheet for board links

acceptance: A board link opens the app when installed, the website when not
Cold start on a link lands on the right board
The association file validates
steps: Serve `apple-app-site-association` from `https://kept.design/.well-known/`, as JSON, no extension, no redirect, correct content type.
Associated Domains entitlement (`applinks:kept.design`) in the app.
Handle `/m/:token` as a cold start, not just while running — the common bug is only handling the warm case.
Anyone without the app must still get the web board. The link is public and sign-in-free by design.
Test from Messages and Notes; Safari's address bar deliberately does not trigger Universal Links.
issues.summary: A board link sent to someone who has the app should open the app, not Safari. It is also the thing that makes the two surfaces feel like one product from the outside.
issues.title: Universal Links for boards

acceptance: An account can be fully deleted from inside the app
No orphaned rows or Storage objects survive
Published board links stop resolving
issues.notes: Worth building on the web app too. The requirement is Apple's, but the capability is not iOS-specific.
steps: A delete path in the app that actually deletes: auth user, rows, and every Storage object.
Confirmation that makes the consequence plain, and is hard to trigger accidentally.
A server-side function does the deletion; the client must not be trusted to cascade it.
Published boards die with the account.
Decide and state the retention position — immediate, or a grace period — and make the copy match what actually happens.
issues.summary: App Store guideline 5.1.1(v): an app that supports account creation must let people delete the account from inside the app. Kept is invite-only and accounts are made by hand, which does not exempt it. This is a common rejection.
issues.title: Delete your account, in the app

acceptance: The manifest covers the app and its dependencies
The privacy answers match what the app actually does
A privacy policy is live at a permanent URL
steps: `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` declaring data types collected and the reasons for any required-reason APIs.
Check the manifests of every third-party SDK that ships in the binary; they aggregate into yours.
Answer the App Store Connect privacy questions honestly: user content, identifiers, what is linked to the user, what is used for tracking (nothing).
A privacy policy at a stable URL on kept.design; the listing requires one.
If location metadata is stripped at import (KEPT-56), say so — it is a genuine selling point.
issues.summary: Apple requires a privacy manifest and accurate data-collection answers. Getting these wrong is both a rejection risk and a trust problem, since the answers are shown publicly on the listing.
issues.title: Privacy manifest and App Store privacy answers

acceptance: The icon reads clearly at the smallest size, in light and dark
Launch does not flash a mismatched colour
Screenshots show the real app
steps: App icon at every required size; test it on both light and dark home screens, and at the smallest size it will ever be drawn.
Launch screen that matches the app's first frame so launch reads as instant rather than as a flash.
App Store screenshots for the required device sizes, showing real collections rather than lorem ipsum.
Listing copy: name, subtitle, description, keywords. The subtitle does a lot of work.
Decide whether the icon reflects the KEPT wordmark or stands apart from it.
issues.summary: The first thing anyone sees, and the last thing anyone leaves time for.
issues.title: App icon, launch screen and store assets

acceptance: A written 4.2 argument exists before submission
Reviewer notes include working credentials and a populated demo account
issues.notes: The demo account is the single most common avoidable rejection for invite-only apps. Set it up before you need it.
steps: Write down the native capabilities the website cannot have: share extension, camera capture, offline library, Universal Links, haptics, background uploads.
Confirm the app is not merely a mirror of kept.design — the IA from KEPT-42 should already differ.
Prepare reviewer notes explaining the invite-only model, with a working demo account. Invite-only apps get rejected for being untestable far more often than for anything else.
Make sure the demo account has real content; an empty library looks broken to a reviewer.
issues.summary: Apple rejects apps that are a website in a wrapper. The rebuild makes this a much easier argument than the Capacitor plan would have, but it is still worth checking deliberately before submitting rather than discovering it in review.
issues.title: Guideline 4.2 readiness review

acceptance: A build is installable from TestFlight on a device that has never been cabled to your Mac
Crashes report with symbols
At least a handful of testers have used it on a real library
steps: EAS production build uploaded to App Store Connect.
Internal testers first (up to 100, no review). External testing needs a beta review, which is lighter than App Store review but not instant.
Builds expire after 90 days — plan the cadence rather than being surprised.
Set up crash reporting before the first tester, not after the first crash.
Ask testers for one specific thing: does it feel good in the hand? Everything else is easier to find yourself.
issues.summary: Real devices, real hands, before the App Store. Also the first time the app runs without a cable and a debugger attached.
issues.title: TestFlight beta

acceptance: The app is on the App Store
A phone-only user can be invited, sign in and build a library end to end
steps: Final build, listing, screenshots, privacy answers and reviewer notes.
Age rating, export compliance (the app uses HTTPS, which is the usual answer), content rights.
Submit, then expect a round of review feedback rather than being surprised by it.
Plan the release: manual release rather than automatic, so the launch happens when you choose.
Tick it off in Kept's own To do page.
issues.summary: The finish line for iOS v1.
issues.title: App Store submission

acceptance: Only opened if a specific, repeated feel problem traces to the framework rather than the implementation
issues.notes: Deliberately parked, not rejected. Reopening this without a concrete failing test from KEPT-44 or KEPT-53 is relitigating D-6.
issues.summary: React Native gets very close to native feel and is not native. If KEPT-53 keeps finding things that cannot be fixed from JavaScript, the ceiling is real and this is the escape hatch.
